title: Holding debates kindly
hookLine: Sikhs discuss authorship and use of parts of it; the Rehat Maryada guides practice

lines: THE GURU'S OWN, OR THE COURT'S?
cards: Two cousins at a wedding, plates in hand, have drifted into an argument about a book. One says every page of it is the Guru's own. The other says some parts may come from poets at the court.
Voices rise a little. An aunt walks over, hands them both a cup of tea, and says, sit down, and say it again, slowly. That scene, in one form or another, is part of Sikh life with the Dasam Granth.
Today isn't about who wins. It's about the tea.

teach.h: WHO WROTE IT? HOW IS IT USED?
teach.b: Here's what Sikhs discuss. First, authorship. Some Sikhs hold that the whole Dasam Granth is the Tenth Guru's own writing.
Others hold that some parts may come from the poets around him, and they weigh each composition on its own. Second, use. Which parts belong in public worship, and which are better left for study?
Sincere Sikhs, scholars and Sikh bodies have come down in different places, and this lesson takes no side.

teach.h: A SHARED CODE KEEPS PRACTICE STEADY.
teach.b: Now notice what keeps daily life steady while the conversation goes on. The Sikh Rehat Maryada, the shared code of conduct, names the compositions that are part of the daily prayers and the Amrit ceremony.

That's the maryada at work. The word means a set way, a proper order, the limits that keep things in shape. So a Sikh can join the morning prayers with the sangat without first settling every question about the book.
The questions stay open; the practice keeps going. And the Gurus left words about how to talk.
Guru Nanak, in a hymn on Ang 661 of the Guru Granth Sahib, says something like this: as long as we're in this world, we should listen to some and say some. Listening first is built right in.
Elsewhere Gurbani warns that speaking harshly makes the heart harsh too. Put those together and you get a way of holding a debate. Say what you think.
Keep the shared practice in the middle, where both of you can stand on it.

how: Sikhs discuss questions about the Dasam Granth in study circles, scholarship and Sikh bodies, while gurdwaras follow the Sikh Rehat Maryada for which compositions are recited in daily prayer and at the Amrit ceremony.

o: keeping a disagreement warm and fair, listening first
avoiding hard questions so nobody gets upset
letting one elder settle every argument for good

games.q: the debate and the code: tap the pairs.
p: the Guru's own, or the court's?

s: Sikhs must settle the authorship question before they pray
the shared code names the daily prayers, so practice goes on while the questions stay open.
Sikhs hold more than one view on parts of the Dasam Granth
some hold it is all the Guru's own; others weigh each composition.
Gurbani says only to speak your mind
Guru Nanak's hymn pairs it: listen to some, say some.

games.q: your cousin disagrees with you about who wrote part of the Dasam Granth. what keeps you both at the same morning prayers?
games.why: the Rehat Maryada names the compositions in the daily prayers, so the debate can stay open while the practice keeps going.

practice: Bring to mind one real disagreement you're in, at home, at work or online, and before you rehearse your side, say their view to yourself in their words until it sounds fair.
Then find one thing you both stand on, and if you pray, ask in your own words for a gentle tongue.
